question: Why is it mistaken to call the multitude of beings insentient?
premises: The multitude of beings forcibly seizes hearts, makes them dance, and conceals the heart of the self in playful gestures.
Such activity shows liveliness rather than insentience.
Calling it insentient reflects the speaker's own dullness, though even that dullness could ironically suggest likeness to the divine play.
inference: The world of beings is not insentient; to call it so is a mistake born of the speaker's own insensitivity.
uncertainties: bhāvavrāta is addressed poetically; it may mean the totality of phenomena or beings.
The final irony about jaḍātmatā as praise is rhetorically compressed.
plain_english: O multitude of beings, you seize people's hearts, make them dance with many gestures, conceal the heart of the self, and play. Anyone who calls you insentient is himself insentient and poorly taught. I would even say that if he has any insentient nature, it could only count as praise insofar as it suggests some likeness to you.
